title: Gina:
headline: In Northern Ireland, peace work started four years before the peace agreement, and it held the peace together.
story: Gina works for the Special EU Programmes Body, created by the Good Friday Agreement. The surprise: their peace programme ran four years before there was peace. Bringing people into one room was not easy then. It gave people hope.

Over 30 years, 23,000 small projects kept going. When politics broke down, ordinary people held the peace together, looking to the future. A concrete, hopeful lesson: start building trust before the agreement.
do: Open on frame 1 on “four years before we actually had peace” with the hook text.
Let the numbers land: 14,000 and 23,000 as plain captions, no graphics.
End on “the future.” Hold half a second.
Name super at 00:07, after the hook.
Cover every trim with B-roll or a soft speech ramp.
dont: Do not use 01:41–02:22 (programme headings). It is admin language.
Do not use 04:25–05:15 (the justice and legacy “mistake”). That is a different video.
No EU programme logos and no programme mechanics.
No camera-shutter sounds. No choppy jump cuts.

transcript:
Auto-transcript of FX6_LVH_6358.MXF (Gina, Brussels, 15 Sep 2026). Times are mm:ss in the source file. Speaker labels are often wrong: 00:51, 01:34 and 07:19 are Gina.
[00:00] Interviewer: Could you tell us about your work in Northern Ireland and the most significant lesson you've learned?
[00:12] Well, we are a body called the Special EU Programmes Body that was actually created
[00:18] as part of the Peace Accord, the Belfast Good Friday Agreement and our statutory remit is
[00:24] to deliver EU programmes called Peace and Reconciliation and we've had those programmes
[00:30] in our region since 1994 and that's a very interesting aspect is that the Good Friday
[00:37] Agreement, the Peace Accord came in 1998 so we had the programme running for four years
[00:45] before we actually had peace and we funded 14,000 projects during that time and in the
[00:51] whole 30 years we've funded 23,000 projects so you can see the importance of those four
[00:57] years and the first programme because they were about building trust and when you look
[01:02] back at some of the things that were actually carried out during that time, they look easy
[01:06] now but they were not easy at that stage post conflict, bringing people in the same room
[01:13] to speak together was not easy but now 30 years later that seems like an easy task.
[01:20] So we've had that programme now running for 30 years and it goes through a series of adaptations,
[01:27] it changes, it has to change as society changes, as the environment changes, economically,
[01:34] how things are, the programme has to adapt and you cannot have one programme that starts
[01:41] from the post conflict the day after a peace accord that is still relevant 30 years later.
[01:47] The headings might be relevant such as support for community infrastructure, victims and
[01:52] survivors, building good relations, positive shared spaces but underneath it all the programme
[01:58] has to change and adapt and evolve and I suppose one of the greatest lessons for us has been
[02:04] that when you start on the process of a post conflict society you don't go from conflict,
[02:11] peace accord, reconciliation, it's much more challenging than that, it's much more complex
[02:17] and we've had to do that but what we try to do now with the investment is make sure that
[02:22] the investment makes a difference, that the actual peace building activity that we're
[02:27] undertaking we consider it an ecosystem of peace building.
[02:32] We look at all different aspects whether it's community relations, business, prosperity,
[02:38] economic opportunities for those most disadvantaged who saw the most of a conflict and unfortunately
[02:46] remain most disadvantaged today.
[02:49] So we try to look at every aspect of peace building and we have learnt so much in those 30 years.
[02:56] Interviewer: What is one peace building approach that you see in work in Northern Ireland that you believe could make a difference in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict?
[03:12] I do believe it's very important that that first programme to have before you have a
[03:19] peace agreement because that first programme as I said might look easy now but it wasn't
[03:25] easy then but it gave people an opportunity to see what peace could look like and it gave
[03:31] people hope in what might be possible and what opportunities they might be able to avail
[03:39] of in the future.
[03:41] So the first programme actually for the majority of people besides being community relations
[03:46] and positive trust building was also very economic so it focused on skills development
[03:53] for people, for those most vulnerable groups as well who hadn't had any chance during the
[03:59] conflict particularly women, vulnerable victims and survivors, young people who maybe weren't
[04:06] getting schooled properly and weren't seeing that in the home and weren't getting educated
[04:12] so that they could go on and build a life for themselves.
[04:15] I think that before the peace accord element of hope and peace building is fundamental
[04:22] for any peace accord.
[04:25]-[05:15] (justice and legacy issues: not used in this video)
[05:15] Ireland but underneath all of that those projects that were funded, those people that were working
[05:21] every day building peace in their communities, in their small ways, held peace together when
[05:29] the political institutions broke down, those people that were working in that support web
[05:36] of 23,000 projects and all the civilians that were involved in those, they were changing,
[05:43] they were looking at themselves, they were looking to a positive future, they weren't
[05:47] just looking at the past, they did have to address the past but they were looking to
[05:51] the future.
[05:54] Interviewer: (question about the international partners)
[06:03]-[07:03] (her thanks to the international partners: not used)
[07:05] The EU was seen as a neutral party, they were able to come in and they imposed regulations
[07:12] and transparency and that opportunity for us to actually push the boat out a bit in
[07:19] what we were trying to do, which the government couldn't do.
[07:24] The objectivity and the transparency then of the programme and answering to our international
[07:31] donors and having them there to advise and shape, I cannot describe the importance of that.
[07:39] It was the international aspect, they were outside of the conflict, they were able to
[07:45] look in and view everybody as equal citizens and that's how the programme then was shaped.
